newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Kazakh grain harvest may be better than forecast.
newsitem.headline: Kazakh grain harvest may be better than forecast.

text.p: Kazakhstan's government expects a better grain harvest this year of 15-16 million tonnes, but the former Soviet republic's agriculture ministry suspects canny farmers might be misleading the statisticians.

"Our farmers are underestimating yields deliberately and giving false figures because of fears that their grain could be taken away from them," agriculture ministry spokesman Alexander Korablin told Reuters.

The government has tried to reassure farmers that it will take only 1.1 million tonnes of grain for state needs, such as the army and hospitals -- grain that was paid for in spring with $165 million of promissory notes.

"The rest can be sold independently by producers," said Korablin. The state offered farmers about $135 per tonne this year for third class soft wheat, the most common grade, compared with a free market or export price of more than $160.
Last year's drought-hit harvest officially totalled 10 million tonnes, which was still enough to cover annual domestic consumption of about eight million tonnes.
The balance is mostly exported to traditional markets in other former Soviet republics, mainly Russia, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan and Turkmenistan.

Private farmers, who recall Stalinist-type requisition measures used in the Soviet era and who are now enjoying the freedom to dispose of their output independently, are often reluctant to disclose crop information to prying officials.
They are also aware that low supplies mean higher prices.
However, no shortages are expected this year despite drought in some western areas and problems with locusts elsewhere which the government managed to localise before any major damage.
Korablin said the agriculture ministry's forecast for the 1996 grain harvest was lower than that of the government and of the economy ministry but still above last year's output.
"This year we can realistically expect 13-14 million tonnes, but it all depends on how the harvest finishes," he said, adding that official estimates did not take account of disingenuous farmers.
Kazakh grain statistics refer to the weight after cleaning and processing. Most of the crop is wheat, although the total includes some rye and barley.

Korablin said the final outcome of the harvest would depend largely on weather in the coming weeks. "We can expect the rain to turn to snow at the end of September, then there will be a brief window for harvesting in October before more rain and snow."
The harvest has been completed in southern and western regions, but farmers in the northern grain belt still have to reap large areas.
There have been better fuel supplies this year than in the past, although shortages of farm equipment, fertilisers and pesticides persist.
